articles.title: Why All-Star Pitcher Could Miss Brewers World Series Roster Despite Being in 'Good Spot' amid Injury
articles.summary: Milwaukee Brewers starting pitcher Brandon Woodruff might not receive a spot on the team's World Series roster.
articles.body:
Milwaukee Brewers starting pitcher Brandon Woodruff might not receive a spot on the team's World Series roster.

According to Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic, the Brewers are fearful that an injury to Woodruff would prevent them from replacing him on their roster due to MLB rules that may determine a health issue as pre-exisiting.

"The rule states a player on a postseason roster can be replaced only if he suffers an acute, non-chronic injury or ailment," Rosenthal reported Tuesday. "The Brewers' fear with Woodruff, according to club officials briefed on his situation, is that any injury he suffers might be viewed as recurring or pre-existing, making the team unable to add another pitcher in his place."

Woodruff hasn't pitched since July 4 due to right shoulder inflammation , but wanted a spot on Milwaukee's World Series roster following its NLCS sweep of the Los Angeles Dodgers.

"It's gonna be hard to keep me off that roster," Woodruff told Curt Hogg of the Milwaukee Journal-Sentinel (h/t Rosenthal).

"I'm going to do everything I can. I'm in a good spot. It means a lot to me," he added. "… I've always believed in myself. It doesn't matter if I've thrown one pitch in two months or if I have 10 rehab outings. I don't care. I feel like I can go out there and do it. I hope I get that opportunity."

The two-time All-Star faced Brewers hitters on Tuesday as he attempts to make his return.

Woodruff made nine starts for Milwaukee during the regular season, owning a 2-2 record to go along with a 2.98 ERA and 0.838 WHIP. He racked up 47 strikeouts compared to 10 walks in 45.1 innings of work.

The Brewers will need to make a decision regarding Woodruff's roster status ahead of Game 1 against the Tampa Bay Rays on Friday.

articles.title: MLB's World Series Records That Will Never Be Broken
articles.summary: The 2026 World Series matchup is officially set. The Milwaukee Brewers will take on the Tampa Bay Rays in a showdown between two teams looking for the first championship in franchise history.
articles.body:
The 2026 World Series matchup is officially set. The Milwaukee Brewers will take on the Tampa Bay Rays in a showdown between two teams looking for the first championship in franchise history.

The beauty of baseball is that, despite the fact that it's been played for more than a century, on any given night, fans might see something they've never seen before and never see again.

Ahead, we've highlighted seven World Series records that will never be broken, spanning individual series records, career records and even game-specific details.

What never-before-seen feat will be accomplished this October?

Over 19 seasons in the big leagues, Yogi Berra played in the World Series 14 times and won 10 rings, one more than fellow Yankees legend Joe DiMaggio for the most ever by a player.

The most rings by a player active in the 2000s is five, held by a handful of players, including Derek Jeter. The active leader is Mookie Betts with four rings from his time with the Red Sox and Dodgers.

Berra did it at a time before the LCS was added. The World Series matchup was simply the AL's best team against the NL's best team. In today's expanded playoff format, a player's chances of suiting up for 10 World Series appearances are virtually nonexistent, let alone winning 10 rings.

While 35 strikeouts might not sound like an insurmountable record, consider for a moment what it took Bob Gibson to put up that record-setting total against the Tigers during the 1968 World Series.

Game 1: 9.0 IP, 5 H, 0 ER, 17 K Game 4: 9.0 IP, 5 H, 1 ER, 10 K Game 7: 9.0 IP, 8 H, 4 ER, 8 K

It's worth noting that Gibson took the loss in Game 7. Facing the same lineup three times increases exposure to hitters who generally don't see the same pitcher in such rapid succession.

Pitch counts are not available, but it's fair to assume Gibson was well into the triple digits in all three starts. It's simply hard to envision any manager riding his ace that hard in today's game, even in pursuit of a title.

For recent comparison, Yoshinobu Yamamoto tossed a complete game, a second quality start and had a 2.2-inning save in last year's World Series to earn MVP honors. He finished with 15 strikeouts.

Not unlike Bob Gibson's 35 strikeouts in a single World Series, this record does not necessarily sound unbreakable at first, but there's a reason no one has come close in recent history.

Yogi Berra (295) and Mickey Mantle (273) are the only players in history with more than 250 plate appearances in the World Series. Derek Jeter (173) is a full 100 short of Mantle's total, despite his status as a fixture in October throughout his Hall of Fame career.

Only six players in MLB history have even reached double-digit home runs in the World Series. Among active players, the co-leaders are George Springer and Freddie Freeman, with seven each.

Springer is tied with Chase Utley and Reggie Jackson for the most home runs in a single World Series with five. Even if a player accomplished that rare feat three different times, he would still be four home runs shy of overtaking Mantle for the top spot.

Record: 1 hour, 25 minutes Record Holder: 1908 World Series, Game 5 (Cubs vs. Tigers)

Considering playoff games today feature roughly 85 minutes of Sydney Sweeney and Megan Fox commercials alone, it's virtually impossible to picture a World Series game being played start to finish in under two hours.

This was actually a series-clinching game for the Cubs, who won 2-0 behind a complete-game shutout from Orval Overall (9 IP, 3 H, 0 ER, 10 K) and three-hit games from Frank Chance and Johnny Evers.

The Cubs actually had 10 hits in the game, which makes the dizzying pace of play even more impressive.

Between commercials and inevitable pitching changes, this one should comfortably stand the test of time.

Shohei Ohtani's plate appearance rundown from last year's 18-inning odyssey in Game 3 of the World Series speaks for itself:

The vast majority of World Series come and go without anyone ever sniffing nine plate appearances in a single game, let alone reaching base that many times in a single contest, so this one is going to be difficult to touch.

The previous record was six times on base, so he didn't just break it. He absolutely demolished it.

Even in an era when starting pitchers were regularly tasked with throwing complete games, especially in October when the season hangs in the balance, it took Whitey Ford a whopping 11 trips to the World Series to tally his record-setting 10 wins.

Pitcher wins, in general, have become an afterthought in an age of openers, bullpen games and five strong innings representing a terrific outing for a traditional starting pitcher.

Yoshinobu Yamamoto was the first pitcher since Randy Johnson in 2001 to record three wins in one World Series last October. He has a fourth win from the 2024 Fall Classic, so he's one to watch.

Still, he's not even halfway there. He won't add to that total this season either. Being 28 years old doesn't help either. Never say never, but a lot will have to break right for him to make a legitimate run at the record.

Records .700 OBP (career) 1.294 SLG (career) 1.994 OPS (career) 13 BB (single-series) 7 IBB (single-series)

The 2002 World Series was the only Fall Classic Barry Bonds played in during his 22-year career. While the Angels came out on top in seven games, Bonds rewrote the record books.

A year after his 73-homer season and in his second of four straight MVP campaigns, Bonds was at the absolute peak of his game. The Angels wanted nothing to do with pitching to him.

He was walked in 13 of his 30 plate appearances. He went 8-for-17 with two doubles, four home runs and six RBI when they gave him something to hit.

Qualifying for the all-time leaderboard requires at least 20 plate appearances. That .700 on-base percentage will be the toughest one for anyone to top. David Ortiz, one of the greatest postseason hitters of all time, sits a distant second on that list at .576.

The Many Pitching Records of a Different Era

Most CG, Single WS: Deacon Phillippe (5, 1903) Most CG, Career: Christy Mathewson (10) Most IP, Single Game: Babe Ruth (14.0, 1916) Most IP, Single WS: Deacon Phillippe (44.0, 1903) Most IP, Career: Whitey Ford (146.0) Most SHO, Single WS: Christy Mathewson (3, 1905) Most SHO, Career: Christy Mathewson (4)

Simply because pitching staffs have transformed over the past 100 years, several pitching records from the early days of the World Series will never be broken.

One of the fascinating records belongs to Babe Ruth, not from his days as a slugger for the Yankees, but as a pitcher for the Red Sox. He tossed all 14 innings of a 2-1 victory over the Brooklyn Robins in Game 2 of the 1916 World Series, allowing six hits and one earned run.

The five complete games thrown by Deacon Phillippe also sounds like something out of a video game. He threw complete games on Oct. 1, 3, 6, 10 and 13, going 3-2 with a 3.07 ERA in 44 innings of work.

articles.title: Ranking Cubs OF Seiya Suzuki, Ian Happ Landing Spots Ahead of MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: The Chicago Cubs let Kyle Tucker walk in free agency last winter due in part to their ability to shift Seiya Suzuki back to right field to fill the void, but there will be no in-house shuffling this time around as Suzuki and left fielder Ian Happ are both set to hit the open market.
articles.body:
The Chicago Cubs let Kyle Tucker walk in free agency last winter due in part to their ability to shift Seiya Suzuki back to right field to fill the void, but there will be no in-house shuffling this time around as Suzuki and left fielder Ian Happ are both set to hit the open market.

Suzuki has been a consistent run producer since joining the Cubs on a five-year, $85 million deal, posting a 131 OPS+ with 26 home runs and a career-high 5.1 WAR in 2026 thanks in part to improved defensive metrics in right field.

Happ is the longest-tenured player on the Cubs roster and a four-time Gold Glove winner in left field. The 32-year-old had a down year at the plate, but still finished with a 103 OPS+ and 55 extra-base hits with 2.9 WAR in 156 games.

Ahead, we've highlighted the most likely landing spots in free agency this winter for the Cubs' tandem, focusing on teams capable of contending with the financial flexibility and positional need at a corner outfield spot or designated hitter to be a logical fit.

The Reds have occasionally been willing to pay for a veteran bat, though it has rarely worked out in their favor, with Mike Moustakas, Jeimer Candelario and Eugenio Suárez this past season among the cautionary tales. The need is clearly there; ownership's willingness to spend is the reason for pause.

The Mets appear to have their present and future outfield in place with Juan Soto and 2026 rookies Carson Benge and A.J. Ewing, but designated hitter is a potential area to upgrade. The DH spot produced a .213/.310/.378 line this past season, and with their limitless budget, a run at signing Suzuki to fill that hole is not out of the question.

The Pirates showed a newfound willingness to spend last winter, though their top priority this offseason is expected to be re-signing Brandon Lowe. That will likely cost them an average annual value of $20 million on a multi-year deal. Even with their newfound financial flexibility, they probably only have one signing on that level on the horizon this winter, making a high-profile outfield upgrade more of a fallback plan.

The Orioles' outfield contingent ranked 28th in the majors with a .229 batting average in 2026, so there is plenty of room to upgrade. The more likely focus will be revamping an underperforming pitching staff that is poised to lose Trevor Rogers in free agency.

The Tigers used 10 different starting right fielders in 2026, with Zach McKinstry (49 starts) and Kerry Carpenter (41 starts) the closest thing they had to regular options at the position. Suzuki's right-handed power bat would be a nice complement to left-handed hitters Riley Greene and Kevin McGonigle, but like the Orioles, rebuilding the starting rotation figures to be their No. 1 priority.

The Astros' outfielders hit a combined .210/.286/.376, and while Cam Smith was the everyday starter in right field, the other two spots were a revolving door. Ideally, they would find a right-handed hitter capable of manning center field. With significant pitching needs as well, the fit here is plausible but not a slam dunk.

The Royals need offensive upgrades and have a clear spot to upgrade in left field. The question is whether they will be willing to spend the money it will take to sign any of the market's top free agents, or if they'll try to patch things together in the bargain bin like they did last winter.

Projected OF: LF Casey Schmitt, CF Drew Gilbert, RF Jung Hoo Lee Projected DH: Bryce Eldridge

Casey Schmitt played a respectable left field (231.2 INN, -4 DRS, -2 OAA), but fits best as a corner infielder or designated hitter, which could ultimately make him a trade chip given the presence of Rafael Devers, Matt Chapman and Bryce Eldridge.

The Giants have been willing to spend in recent years, and while they need some help for Logan Webb in the starting rotation, adding a defensive standout like Happ to their spacious outfield or a power bat like Suzuki to the middle of their underperforming lineup could also provide a major boost.

A Possible Trade Made by Every Team This Offseason ⚾

Japanese 'Triple Crown' winner coming to MLB

Projected OF: LF Brandon Marsh, CF Justin Crawford, RF Gabriel Rincones Jr. Projected DH: Kyle Schwarber

The Phillies took a flier on Adolis García last offseason hoping he could be a buy-low solution to their need for a right-handed hitting outfielder, but a torn lat muscle ended his season in June. Right field was a black hole until Bryce Harper moved back there following the deadline addition of Luis Arraez.

With Arraez set to depart in free agency, it's a clear position of need once again, and Suzuki figures to be one of the top targets for the Phillies this winter. The big question is just how much more this team is willing to spend on aging veteran talent, and whether shoring up the bullpen around Jhoan Durán will be a bigger priority.

Projected OF: LF Michael Arroyo, CF Julio Rodríguez, RF Dominic Canzone Projected DH: Lazaro Montes

Randy Arozarena might be headed for a $100 million payday as arguably the top bat on the free-agent market this winter, and there's a good chance that contract will be coming from someone other than the Mariners.

Suzuki likely won't come much cheaper, at least from an AAV standpoint, but he might be available on a shorter deal. Meanwhile, Happ could be a great fit in left field where his defense, extra-base pop and clubhouse leadership give him some buy-low upside after a down year.

Projected OF: LF Nathan Lukes, CF Brett Bateman, RF Addison Barger Projected DH: Sean Keys

"This offseason, said a league source who spoke on condition of anonymity in order to discuss offseason plans, the Jays are expected to pursue Chicago Cubs outfielder Seiya Suzuki," wrote Mitch Bannon of The Athletic in late September.

With Addison Barger coming off a season where he played just nine games and George Springer headed for free agency and perhaps retirement, a corner outfielder and a designated hitter will both be on the offseason shopping list.

Projected OF: LF Matt Shaw, CF Pete Crow-Armstrong, RF Kevin Alcántara Projected DH: BJ Murray Jr.

Suzuki and Happ are not the only Cubs outfielders headed for free agency this winter, as veteran Michael Conforto and platoon standout Tyrone Taylor are also free agents, leaving the club with multiple holes to fill in both the starting lineup and on the bench.

They could give Matt Shaw a regular home in the outfield after he filled a super-utility role in 2026, but there's a good chance they will pursue a reunion with Suzuki, and if Happ is willing to accept a hometown discount, both could return.

After ranking as the top offense and top defense in baseball this season, there's no reason for the Cubs to be hunting for sweeping changes to their position player group, even if the offense went cold in October.

articles.title: Rays, Brewers Head Into 2026 World Series With Many Connections
articles.summary: Drew Rasmussen, Freddy Peralta, Jake Bauers and Ozzie Timmons are among connections between the 2026 World Series teams.
articles.body:
Ozzie Timmons was the Milwaukee Brewers' hitting coach for three seasons before returning to the Tampa Bay Rays in 2025 for a second stint on manager Kevin Cash's staff. He had plenty of good things to say about Freddy Peralta the day the righthanded pitcher was acquired from the New York Mets at this season's trade deadline.

"He's a great teammate, a competitor and he works hard," said Timmons , who is Cash's assistant hitting coach, a Tampa native, a former University of Tampa superstar and played in a dozen games for the Rays in 2000. "He's a good person, a family man, has a lot of energy."

Peralta spent his first eight seasons in the majors with Milwaukee and was a two-time all-star, including 2025 when he won 17 games. In his short time with the Rays, Peralta been nothing less than sensational. That is especially the case since late August when he began a current stretch in which he is 7-0 with a 0.89 ERA in 10 appearances (nine starts) with the Rays winning all 10.

Peralta, who won a pair of games and had an effective relief outing against Cleveland en route to winning ALCS MVP honors, and Timmons are among a number of connections between the Rays and Brewers.

Timmons compared Peralta's healthy clubhouse disposition to that of current Giants' shortstop Willy Adames, who also played for both clubs and was a teammate of Peralta's in Milwaukee. (More on Adames below.)

Here are few more connections and similarities between the teams.

Rays or Brewers will be first-time World Series winner

Only five of 30 MLB teams have not won a World Series. The short list will whittle down to four with either the Rays, a 1998 expansion team, or the Brewers, who got their start as the Seattle Pilots in 1969 before moving to Milwaukee for the 1970 season, achieving a franchise first.

The others who have yet to enjoy a late-October champagne soaking are the San Diego Padres (1969), Seattle Mariners (1977) and Colorado Rockies (1993).

To accommodate the expansion Tampa Bay Devils Rays' residency in the American League East and that of fellow expansion partner, the Arizona Diamondbacks, in the National League West, some realignment was engineered to maintain an even number of teams in each league. With Tampa Bay on board, the Detroit Tigers shifted from the AL East to the AL Central. The Brewers moved from the AL Central to the NL Central to boost the National League's inventory to 16 teams and keep the American League's at 14. (The Astros moved from the NL Central to the AL West in 2013 to give each league 15 teams.)

The above realignment made the World Series that will begin Friday night in Milwaukee possible.

Tampa Bay's staff ace and Cy Young contender was selected in the sixth round of the 2018 draft by Milwaukee out of Oregon State. Rasmussen appeared in 27 games, all in relief, during the 2020 and 2021 seasons. It was during the latter campaign that he was dealt to the Rays along with fellow righthanded reliever J.P. Feyereisen for the aforementioned Adames and pitcher Trevor Richards.

Rasmussen joined the Rays' rotation in the latter stages of 2021, which set him up for a nice 2022 season when he won 11 games with a 2.84 ERA. He was off to a nice start (4-2, 2.62) in 2023 when he was shelved for the duration of that year as well as the first four months of 2024 thanks to having a third elbow procedure, which was of the non-Tommy John variety.

The Washington state native worked his way back, joined the Rays' bullpen in August 2024. He returned to the rotation in 2025 and went 10-5 with a 2.76 ERA 31 starts while having his workload (150 IP) carefully monitored.

With no governor holding him back, 'Ras' flourished this season. He went 16-5 to finish second in the American League in wins, posted a league-best 0.91 WHIP, a 1.67 BB/9 rate that was second to teammate Nick Martinez, and a 2.67 ERA that was good for fourth. The performance carried into the postseason where the 31-year-old is 2-0 with a 1.29 ERA in three starts.

Adames helped lead the Brewers to the postseason in 2021 when he posted an .885 OPS in 99 games after the trade, 2023 and 2024.

The lefty-swinging Bauers was part of a seven-player trade with San Diego that brought him to the Tampa Bay organization in 2014, one year after he was drafted by the Padres. He made his MLB debut with the Rays in 2018, hitting 11 homers and posting a .700 OPS in 96 games.

That off-season, Bauers was included in a three-team swap that sent him and $5 million from the Rays to Indians, Edwin Encarnacion and a draft pick from the Indians to the Mariners, and Carlos Santana from the Mariners to the Indians. Who did the Rays get? Yandy Diaz from Cleveland. Reliever Cole Sulser was also sent to Tampa Bay by Cleveland, and the righthander is in his second stint with the Rays.

Bauers spent less than two full seasons in Cleveland before he was dealt to Seattle. From there, it was off to the Yankees, who sent him to Milwaukee in November 2023 for a pair of minor leaguers.

The 31-year-old Bauers entered this season with a .211 career average. Hence, his .266 was rather stunning. The best season of his career also included 26 homers, 86 RBI and an .873 OPS, which was 150 points above his career mark. His .389 on base percentage was third in MLB.

Colton Gordon has never been employed by the Rays and is not on Milwaukee's active roster. The lefty pitcher, who was acquired from the Astros in mid-July along with Lance McCullers, Jr., is a St. Pete native. Gordon grew up a Tampa Bay fan and faced the Rays in Tampa at Steinbrenner Field last season when the club was forced out of the Trop due to damage sustained from Hurricane Milton.

Steinbrenner Field is adjacent to Hillsborough College where Gordon pitched in 2019. The campus is the location of the Rays' new ballpark, which is scheduled to open for business in 2029. McCullers, like his father, is a Tampa native.

articles.title: 2026 MLB Free Agents Rumors, Predictions for Tarik Skubal, Jazz Chisholm Jr., More
articles.summary: The 2026 MLB offseason offers quite a bit of mystery.
articles.body:
The 2026 MLB offseason offers quite a bit of mystery.

Much of it is, of course, unfortunately wrapped around all the unknowns of the collective bargaining agreement negotiations. That said, a good deal is still tied to the whos, whats and wheres of free agency.

Because there are still impact players available and teams in need of that impact. And with just two teams left in the World Series chase, we're hearing more rumblings about those players and their suitors, so let's break down the buzz.

Jazz Chisholm Jr. has already expressed his desire to remain with the New York Yankees. Unfortunately for him, it continues to sound like that interest is not mutual.

The Athletic's Chris Kirschner was the latest insider to dash Chisholm's dream. While breaking down New York's offseason outlook, Kirschner noted that "it would be surprising" if the Yankees gave qualifying offers to both of their realistic candidates: Chisholm and David Bednar. Kirschner then went on to describe Bednar as "the likelier candidate" to get one.

Per Kirschner, the risk of the Yankees giving Chisholm a qualifying offer is that "he could accept it and try to reset his market entering the 2028 free-agent class." Kirschner also opined that it "spoke volumes when the Yankees benched Chisholm in an elimination game during the American League Division Series."

Maybe if Chisholm was coming off of a stronger season, New York would have interest in keeping him around. But just about everything that could go wrong did, as his power regressed, his contact decreased and he battled both inconsistency and injury. He is a good bounce-back candidate for someone, but that someone won't be the Bombers.

Prediction: Chisholm signs with the Los Angeles Angels.

Mets Preparing Blank-Check Pursuit of Tarik Skubal?

Little went right for the New York Mets this season, but one of the more crushing blows was Freddy Peralta's inability to anchor their rotation.

So, did that sour the Mets on the idea of pursuing an external ace? Not at all. In fact, New York seems to be bracing for a big-money run at the best pitcher on the board in two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal.

"The general consensus among those in the Mets organization and those who deal with (president of baseball operations David) Stearns' front office regularly seems to be that if (owner Steve) Cohen decides he wants Skubal, the Mets will pay whatever it takes to get him," SNY's Chelsea Janes said. "So trying to predict whether Skubal will be a Met next year, then, might be as simple as whether Skubal wants them."

If Skubal wants the biggest paycheck possible, then the Mets might have a real chance. They seem as likely as anyone to slide that kind of offer across the table. If he wants familiarity, though, or perhaps a clearer shot at contention, that could hurt New York, since two of his other primary suitors (the Los Angeles Dodgers and Detroit Tigers) already have an established relationship with him.

Prediction: Skubal re-signs with the Los Angeles Dodgers.

The free agent pool possibly just had a cannon-ball splash courtesy of Japan.

The Hanshin Tigers of Nippon Professional Baseball announced they will approve the posting of star slugger Teruaki Sato this offseason. That means this crop of position players, which appeared light on high-end talent, just had a Triple Crown winner added to it.

Sato, 27, hit .306 this season with 39 home runs and 106 RBI. Previous reports indicated his list of suitors was believed to include the New York Mets, New York Yankees, Los Angeles Dodgers and Philadelphia Phillies.

Sato's list of landing spots likely runs even deeper, but those are all logical choices given their willingness to spend and their need to add talent after disappointing outcomes this season.

Prediction: Sato signs with the Philadelphia Phillies.

articles.title: Brian Cashman Says He's Finalizing Yankees Contract Extension, 'We're Locked and Loaded'
articles.summary: Much to the consternation of a lot of fans in the Bronx, the New York Yankees won't have a new leader in the front office.
articles.body:
Much to the consternation of a lot of fans in the Bronx, the New York Yankees won't have a new leader in the front office.

General manager Brian Cashman announced Wednesday he is finalizing a new deal to remain in the role he has occupied since 1998.

"We're locked and loaded," Cashman said.

The news doesn't come as a big surprise. ESPN's Buster Olney reported on Oct. 8 the signs were pointing toward the return of both Cashman and manager Aaron Boone. Cashman maintains a strong relationship with both Boone and team owner Hal Steinbrenner.

To justify keeping his job, the GM can point to a third straight 90-win season and ninth trip to the playoffs in 10 years. There aren't many other MLB franchises that have been as consistent in the regular season.

But the Yankees aren't an organization that's judged by how much they win in the regular season.

The Bronx Bombers have just one World Series title since their dynastic run from the 1990s into the early 2000s ended, and we're creeping toward a drought of nearly two decades since their last triumph in 2009.

For a lot of fans, that's simply unacceptable, and Cashman is one constant through the fallow period.

Add that to how long he has been the GM overall and it's not unreasonable to ask whether the time had arrived for a major change to the front office.

Not to mention, there's one area of roster-building in which the Yankees continue to fall short. Their defense was once again an issue in 2026. If it's something Cashman has tried to address, he has done a terrible job of it.

If George Steinbrenner were running the show, Cashman may have been axed a long time ago. Nobody has mistaken Hal for his father. He has consistently adopted a more patient, measured approach while running the show.

Steinbrenner and Cashman have clearly remained in alignment, and the Yankees' player development record is likely a factor in ownership's conviction in maintaining the status quo.

Presumptive Cy Young winner Cam Schlittler was a Yankees draft pick in 2022. Ben Rice, Spencer Jones, Austin Wells, George Lombard Jr. and Anthony Volpe all began their careers in the farm system too.

Despite rarely having high draft selections, the organization is cycling talent up through the minors and up to the big leagues.

For fans accustomed to seeing New York pay a premium for proven talent, that only goes so far. And the clock is ticking with three-time MVP Aaron Judge turning 35 next April. There should be some urgency to capitalize on what's left of his prime playing years.

This winter, don't expect the Yankees to be massive spenders in free agency because Tarik Skubal is the only marquee star hitting the market. The battle over a new collective bargaining agreement has all 30 teams in a holding pattern as well.

More than likely this offseason will be business as usual for Cashman because a new contract gives him even less incentive to deviate from his past approach.

Maybe some improvements around the margins are all it takes for the Yankees to be World Series winners in 2027.

articles.title: Aaron Judge's Injury Updated by Yankees' Brian Cashman After Sitting Out 2026 MLB Playoffs
articles.summary: New York Yankees general manager Brian Cashman is expecting star slugger Aaron Judge to be ready for spring training in 2027.
articles.body:
New York Yankees general manager Brian Cashman is expecting star slugger Aaron Judge to be ready for spring training in 2027.

Cashman told reporters the Yankees and Judge "feel like we're in a good place" regarding the rib injury that caused him to miss the entire playoffs:

One player can only do so much, but Judge undoubtedly would've made a difference for New York when two of its three losses to the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League Division Series came by one run.

Yankees hitters combined to bat .130 and slug .239 in the sweep. Cody Bellinger had one hit in 12 at-bats, while Jazz Chisholm Jr. and Trent Grisham were hitless altogether.

Judge's shadow certainly loomed as the Bronx Bombers' offense dried up.

There's nothing that can be done about it now. The hope for New York moving forward is that the three-time AL MVP returns to form in 2027.

A .241/.360/.511 slash line and a 140 OPS+ would be good for a lot of batters. In the case of Judge, this year was his worst offensive campaign since his 2017 breakout.

Maybe the 34-year-old was simply snakebitten as various injuries forced him to miss 96 games in the regular season. His age is going to become a bigger and bigger consideration, though.

If Judge's production is beginning to decline, even gradually, it's going to be a serious concern for the Yankees.

articles.title: Yankees owner Hal Steinbrenner backs manager Aaron Boone's return for 2027: 'I think he had a good year managing-wise'
articles.summary: Boone will manage the Yankees in 2027 with his contract set to expire after the season.
articles.body:
Aaron Boone will be returning as manager of the New York Yankees for the 2027 season, the final year of his contract, the team confirmed on Wednesday.

Owner Hal Steinbrenner and general manager Brian Cashman met with reporters via a video conference to discuss the 2026 season and Boone's future, which faced much speculation after the Yankees' latest postseason exit.

The roster put together by Cashman, who confirmed he has agreed to a contract extension, and the managing job by Boone were backed by Steinbrenner. The Yankees owner praised the team's pitching, but expressed multiple times that the offense was the biggest reason why the team fell short of championship expectations.

"Every year I'm going to look at the situation," Steinbrenner said of contemplating Boone's future. "I don't think you can pin the season and the unacceptable end to it on Aaron. I don't think you can pin it on [Cashman], based on the roster he put together. The offense, not the pitching, but the offense, had a big part of why, in my opinion, why we didn't get where we strive to get every year and we're certainly striving to get this year.

"That was during the whole year. In the postseason, if you look at their performance against the two starting Boston pitchers and their performance against probably all the Rays pitchers, it was just not good. I don't know how else to put it. If you don't score runs, you're not going to win. We all know that."

Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Basketball league for the 2026-27 NBA season

Steinbrenner added that he had a week-long conversation about Boone's status, but in the end did not believe the manager was part of the problem either.

"I don't believe he was," Steinbrenner said. "I think he had a good year managing-wise. I would, of course, consider moving on from Aaron Boone if I thought he was a huge part of the problem and I can certainly, without mentioning names, point out to other managers of other clubs that have been part of the problem and that's why a change was made.

"This year, I just don't believe that's the case."

Boone's contract set to expire after 2027 season

Boone signed a two-year extension through the 2027 MLB season in February 2025 , months after the Yankees lost the World Series to the Los Angeles Dodgers. After two straight eliminations in the ALDS , some expected Boone's time would be up in New York after nine seasons. Instead, he will manage the team through at least the end of his current deal.

The 2026 season saw the Yankees finish second in the AL East for the second straight season and win 90 games for the seventh time in a full season under Boone. It's in the postseason that the Yankees have fallen short more often than not under the 53-year-old.

The Yankees hold a 27-30 playoff record under Boone, which includes three trips to the ALCS and one World Series appearance. His teams are 18-5 as the higher seed in a series and 9-25 as the lower seed. The Yankees were the No. 4 seed in 2026 and beat the No. 5 seed Boston Red Sox in the wild-card round before being swept by the top-seeded Tampa Rays in the ALDS.

Without Aaron Judge and with Giancarlo Stanton available only as a pinch-hitter, the Yankees batted .130 in the ALDS, and three of their five RBI came from Ben Rice. Their pitching was what kept them in games, as evidenced by a 1.88 team ERA, 0.81 team WHIP and a .173 opponent batting average.

"I thought Boone managed a good season, especially with the pitching staff," said Steinbrenner. "He got us to the playoffs, and the bottom-line is the players didn't live up to their end of the bargain in the playoffs."

In the playoffs, other teams have often been able to pick up on the weaknesses of Boone's Yankees teams. The Dodgers told their players their 2024 World Series opponents were "talent over fundamentals" and were bound to self-destruct. Toronto Blue Jays announcer Buck Martinez labeled the AL East rivals as "not a good team" last season, saying they were mistake-prone in the field and on the bases.

Those criticisms were only hardened after seeing Austin Wells' baserunning mistake in Game 1 of the ALDS against the Rays and the Yankees' defensive breakdown in Game 2.

Cashman has been in charge for 29 seasons. Boone is just the third manager to work under him. The Yankees last won the World Series in 2009 and are in the midst of a 17-year championship drought. The boos heard after Trent Grisham's series-ending strikeout against the Rays showed how frustrated the fan base is with the team's current state.

But regardless of their feelings, Cashman apparently isn't ready to hire a new manager just yet. It's unclear what major changes he will make this winter, if any, in hopes of returning the franchise to contender status, which remains the goal of ownership.

"That is our mission, that is our goal," Steinbrenner said.

articles.title: Yankees' Steinbrenner Defends Aaron Boone, Says Players 'Didn't Live Up to Their End of the Bargain'
articles.summary: New York Yankees chairman Hal Steinbrenner directed blame toward players, not general manager Brian Cashman or manager Aaron Boone, for his club's ALDS elimination.
articles.body:
New York Yankees chairman Hal Steinbrenner directed blame toward players, not general manager Brian Cashman or manager Aaron Boone, for his club's ALDS elimination.

Steinbrenner expressed faith in Boone in a Wednesday press conference during which he confirmed an upcoming extension for Cashman.

"I thought Boone managed a good season, especially with the pitching staff," Steinbrenner said (h/t SNY Yankees).

Steinbrenner continued, "He got us to the playoffs, and the bottom line is, the players didn't live up to their end of the bargain in the playoffs."

The Yankees were eliminated from the postseason Oct. 7 after getting swept from the divisional series by the Tampa Bay Rays.

The run marked the club's second consecutive ALDS elimination, and the third straight season during which the Yankees have won more than 90 games but fallen short of a title.

Steinbrenner said Wednesday he felt the blame for that early exit could be directed toward an offense that batted a combined .130 with a dozen hits and five total runs in three games against the Rays.

"I don't think you can pin the season, and the unacceptable end to it, on Aaron," Steinbrenner said. "I don't think you can pit it on [Cashman] based on the roster he put together.

"Again, the offense, not the pitching but the offense, had a big part, in my opinion, of why we didn't get— and I don't mind saying it— where we strive to get every year."

Steinbrenner concluded , "I absolutely believe we had a team that was capable of winning a championship."

Cashman, who has served as general manager of the Yankees since 1998, said Wednesday he was finalizing an extension with the club.

Steinbrenner said as of Wednesday he had not discussed a similar contract with Boone, although the Yankees had held an internal "weeklong conversation" about the managerial position.

He added he did not see Boone as "a huge part of the problem" and was willing to consider an extension going forward.

Boone is currently heading into the final season of his contract in 2027, per MLB.com's Brent Maguire .

Steinbrenner concluded he ultimately refused to look at the season as "a complete failure" despite not returning to the World Series, in which the Yankees last competed in 2024 before suffering elimination at the hands of the Los Angeles Dodgers.

"Winning 93 games is not a failure. Playing in the division series is not a failure," Steinbrenner said. "It became a failure because we did not do well."

The Yankees still succeeded in attracting fans last season despite the club's continued lack of postseason success. Listed in March as the most lucrative team in baseball with an $8.5 billion valuation by Forbes , the Yankees ranked second only to the Dodgers in average attendance this season by drawing crowds of more than 41,700 to the Bronx.

Steinbrenner named Ben Rice as a "bright spot" but said he would overall be looking at his offense from "top to bottom."

"This has been twice, now, where the offense just hasn't lived up to their end of the bargain," Steinbrenner said.

Those comments could potentially offer some insight into how Cashman plans to approach the 10 players he has hitting free agency after this disappointing end to the 2026 season.

It seems likely the Yankees could prioritize retaining pitcher David Bednar over players like Trent Grisham and Jazz Chisholm, who could potentially be walking should the Yankees look to overhaul their offense this winter.

articles.title: Jeff Passan: Brewers-Rays World Series Won’t Head Off MLB Lockout
articles.summary: Passan also addressed the backlash he received to comments about the Dodgers.
articles.body:
ESPN MLB insider Jeff Passan spoke to Front Office Sports about a wide range of topics, including whether a small-market World Series matchup between the Brewers and Rays could help curtail the looming lockout, backlash to previous comments he made about the Dodgers, and the momentum of his ESPN/Omaha Productions podcast, Sources Tell Jeff Passan .

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Front Office Sports : In your estimation, does this small market World Series matchup do anything to potentially curtail or shorten the looming lockout this offseason?

JP: I wish the answer was yes, but I think part of it is because both sides are just so deeply entrenched in their positions that if the inverse of what we're going on right now is true, and this was the Dodgers and Yankees, the MLBPA wouldn't be deviating from its position either, because everyone believes what they want to believe when it comes to a salary cap and moving anyone off of their standard and set position at this point and perhaps going even further is just an impossibility, especially this early on.

So while it would be nice, I think for everybody to acknowledge the reasonable points that the other side is making, no one's prepared to do that at this point. It's what makes this so scary, I think, for baseball long-term. It's a possibility that they are going to remain in their corners and no one's going to want to come meet in the middle. And when that happens, the possibility of this lockout extending even deeper and games being lost becomes that much more realistic.

FOS: Both the Brewers and the Rays have very robust analytics departments, and they also just seem filled top to bottom with gamers. Are we seeing in real-time the melding of new-school analytics and old-school, personality-based eye test type scouting?

JP: I don't know that this is an in real-time thing because the Rays, especially, throughout the years have always leaned pretty heavily on their scouts. They have a big scouting department, and especially on the pro side. This postseason, they were running like four and five-deep scouts at multiple games. And it's not just guys who are traditional scouts. It's somebody like Brandon Hyde, who managed for the Orioles for a few years and who has a good relationship with the people in the front office there. And so they'll deploy him. Or it's a younger guy like Mike Ford, the former Yankee, who went to Princeton and wanted to get to a front office. And the Rays, essentially, just hire a few young former ballplayers, whose minds they whose minds they appreciate, and whose open mindedness they see as suitable and let them loose in roles that are yet to be defined.

So, when you have forward-thinking front offices, especially in smaller markets, they understand there can be a pretty significant return on investment if you spend a little bit extra money.

The Rays, they're not really spending it on payroll, but on infrastructure, that's an area in which they feel like they've found an advantage. And what that winds up doing is there are organizations out there that believe what you get from analytical models is enough to make good decisions. But with the Brewers and I think particularly the Rays, they feel like the more information that you can have, whether it's something that comes out of a computer or something that comes from people's eyes, there is a pretty distinct benefit to that.

FOS : In the big picture, it's really hard to criticize the Brewers' front office given what they've accomplished with the resources that they have. But I look at this Freddy Peralta trade. And for this season, they've gotten negative value back. Brandon Sproat was pretty brutal, getting pulled in the middle of at-bats for command issues. Jett Williams seems to be like number seven or eight on their middle infield depth chart, and now they're facing Peralta, albeit on a different team than the one they traded him to, in the World Series, and he's been dynamite. Does this have the potential to really bite them? The combo of not having him as their second or third starter, and having to go against him?

JP: The way Freddy Peralta is pitching right now, absolutely. But the Brewers have almost made this form of trade, getting rid of a guy on the eve of his free agency or in the year going into when he's going to be a free agent, part of their strategy.

And I think it illustrates where a lot of the frustration is among fans, especially in smaller market teams. It's not necessarily that the Dodgers and the Mets are specifically spending that much more money than everyone else.

It's the function of that, which is that when it comes to free agency, a lot of these organizations like the Brewers or even like the Rays, who have done this plenty as well, just believe they're not going to be able to afford these players and so they try and extract as much value out of them as they can. Now, could they afford them?

Yeah, I think that both the Rays and the Brewers could have larger payrolls, and especially the Rays and we would see that guarantee in a capped system and we would not necessarily see that guarantee with what the players want and is that gap at the bottom between the lower spending teams and the floor enough to make up for what they've lost at the top end?

Major League Baseball said yes. The Players Association doesn't believe that MLB's proposal is equivalent in that regard at all. When it comes to this labor dispute, there are two very different interpretations of the same set of facts and it's part of what's so frustrating, I think, for common fans that even though they want to understand this, doing so takes time and and it takes an investment in knowledge and fans, they just wanna watch their teams play—and their favorite players—and the vast majority are not going to dive into the minutiae that is labor relations.

FOS : We've been talking about the Dodgers a bit. Earlier this season, if you'll recall, there was a lot of backlash for things that you have said in the past about the Dodgers and how everybody could utilize their resources like they do. How much of this pushback, which happened amid revelations of complex financial issues with the Dodger ownerships and their other businesses, that you got on social media was valid in your opinion, and how much of it do you think was unfair and/or taken out of context?

JP: This is a subject that gets people extremely passionate, so I understand entirely that in my role, there's not a duty necessarily to be a voice for the fans, but at the very least to reflect the position of dissatisfaction, and I didn't do a good enough job of that.

There were things that I regret not looking into when it comes to what the Dodgers did and how they went out and did it, but I don't think that invalidates some of the points that I was trying to make, and clearly not making elegantly enough. Because I think that there are a lot of teams that could stand to be more like the Dodgers in the way that, with the resources they have, they go out and pursue players.

Can other teams go and splash cash around the way that the Dodgers have with signing bonuses or putting hundreds of millions of dollars a year into deferred salaries? No. But, I don't want to undersell either the idea that there are a lot of people and a lot of teams that could be spending more of the money that they have right now.

And I think the perfect illustration of this is what David Rubenstein, the new Orioles owner, said in front of an economic forum where, and I'm paraphrasing here, he said, "I saw everybody in baseball making more money than I was making in private equity. I wanted to join the party." I appreciate very much David Rubenstein's honesty because when you see an owner say the quiet part out loud, it at least suggests that the idea that these teams are doing very, very well compared to what a lot of owners will say publicly and what Major League Baseball will say, it just counteracts the perspectives publicly that they all have espoused.

FOS : That being said, do Dodgers fans have some real reason for concern between an aging roster, new MLB rules potentially coming in, all of this deferred money coming due, and all of these other financial issues that the Dodgers owners are facing outside of the team?

JP: I'll get to the deferred money first because I don't think that's quite as material as all of the other things, unless for some reason they don't have the cash to fund that deferred money. Because remember, deferrals, it pushes off into the future what is owed, but it does so by two years at best. You still need to put in a large chunk of money to then go and earn interest and eventually in that account have enough money to pay off that deferred compensation. So I think that's in a slightly different category.

Mark Walter's potential legal jeopardy, as much as the Dodgers and people at MLB have suggested that it's probably not going to affect the Dodgers, it absolutely can. If there are indictments handed down, if there are questions about cash flow, if there's efforts to untangle the enormous web that is Guggenheim and bring a little bit more opacity to the situation in baseball, then yeah, that could potentially impede the Dodgers from operating the way that they have in recent seasons.

And if the Dodgers aren't spending as much money or if the Dodgers are, say, a little bit more loath to go out there with those over the top signings like Kyle Tucker at $60 million a year was, or like getting Tanner Scott and Edwin Díaz to close in back-to-back offseasons, yeah, that combined with an aging roster could squeeze them a little bit, but we also can't forget the Dodgers have one of the five best farm systems in baseball. And while it is top heavy with hitters at this point, one thing that the Dodgers have done relatively well is maybe not develop long-term starting pitching, but develop arms that contribute at the big-league level whether it's Justin Wrobleski or Emmet Sheehan and just find those sorts of guys.

So the Dodgers I don't think anytime soon are gonna fall into a situation where they're in the doldrums, this is not going to be a rebuild waiting to happen because Freddie Freeman is getting older and going to be a free agent sooner because Teoscar Hernández is getting older or even Shohei Ohtani is getting older. They have enough there to compliment them on this beat.

FOS: Your podcast with ESPN and Omaha has a lot of momentum. It won Signal awards recently. What's it been like to really embrace this form of storytelling as another tool in your tool belt between writing and scoops and TV?

JP: An incredible, incredibly fulfilling challenge. And this sort of thing doesn't come naturally to me necessarily, so I'm learning it on the fly and trying to understand what works and what doesn't, what people want to see and hear and what they don't.

And it's been really fulfilling because it's challenging. And I love that. I don't naturally understand how something works or don't have the learned experience through doing it for as many years as I have been writing or doing TV. Learning on the fly is tough and it makes me nimble and it gives me the sorts of new skills that I need to be as well-rounded a modern journalist as I possibly can be. And I sometimes ask myself is it really necessary to do all of these things? Because you see other writers and reporters who have gone more into the multimedia space and they don't write and report quite as much as they used to. And the truth is, maybe it's not necessary, but it's sure fun.

articles.title: MLB took over Brewers broadcasts this year. The ratings went way up
articles.summary: MLB says the Brewers' in-market ratings soared 25% in 2026, a good sign for the new regime of MLB-produced broadcasts.
articles.body:
The 2026 Milwaukee Brewers season was unlike any that came before, with the team racking up 103 wins and reaching the World Series. It also looked unlike any that came before, thanks to a change in broadcast.

With Major League Baseball overtaking the game-broadcast production for eight teams this year after the financial troubles of Main Street Sports (the company that oversaw the Bally Sports Wisconsin branding), Brewers games got a makeover, and the ratings reflected a renewed interest in the product.

Brewers local viewership, including "linear" (people watching on cable or satellite) and "streaming" (people watching with the app), was up 25%, according to MLB. Among the 29 U.S. teams, the Brewers had the top market rating of 6.29, which essentially means 6% of televisions inside the market were turned to Brewers games when they were on.

It does bear mentioning that Nielsen changed its national metric recording process in early September 2025 , meaning it switched to what it considers more accurate data collection after most of the 2025 season had been played, but that didn't impact local data collection.

A tweak was made to the local data-collection process in September 2026, meaning one month of the 2026 numbers could be slightly impacted. For the most part, the 2025 and 2026 numbers in Milwaukee were collected under the same system.

The upgrade in broadcast quality has been a noticeable development in 2026.

"I think the telecasts are a lot better these days, and a lot of people are really tuning in," said Billy Chambers, executive vice president of local media with MLB. "Another big thing is the timing of the game. The game moves along so much better, and that helps attendance.

"If you add up the total of number minutes [people in the market who watched Brewers baseball], it outranks any television show, cable and broadcast."

The Brewers went all-in on the improvements available through the MLB production , including a drone camera, ump camera, dirt camera and more. Access went up, from in-game interviews to handheld cameras following players through a gauntlet of high-fives in the dugout after a home run.

The Brewers aren't the only team to see a marked increase. The Colorado Rockies , who moved from a provider that wasn't as widely available as broadcasts are now, saw a viewership increase of 49%, even in a down season. The St. Louis Cardinals (29%), Cleveland Guardians (28%) and Brewers (25%) all went way up, as well. In all, 11 of the 14 teams whose broadcasts are handled by MLB went up with the combined linear and streaming numbers.

It was impressive for MLB, considering it added eight teams to its portfolio when Main Street collapsed, on fairly short notice before the 2026 season.

"The big thing that we preach to our group is we want to be stewards of the team's brand," Chambers said. "We work really hard with the teams for access to the players, that's what really drives it. The Brewers were 100 percent behind this new technology … that technology will only get better."

Across baseball, MLB said viewership was up 10%, boosted by a huge season from Toronto on Sportsnet after the Blue Jays reached the World Series last year. The Brewers, of course, had a huge season on the field, too, though they've been riding a wave of success in the past five years, so that wasn't entirely novel.

Weekday attendance across baseball was also up 13%, something MLB spokesman Matt Bourne credited at least in part to a faster-moving game and relative certainty that a contest will be over in three hours or less.

The Brewers' in-person attendance of 2,788,933 ranked 11th across Major League Baseball, up from 12th last year when Milwaukee brought 2,650,089 through the gates. It's an increase of 5% from 2025. It's also the highest the Brewers have finished in the MLB rankings since 2021 and the highest turnout since 2019.

Fox declares NLCS a huge ratings winners

Keep that previous Nielsen caveat in mind, but Fox sports touted the National League Championship Series between the Brewers and Dodgers to be the best viewership of any LCS on any network since 2015.

That's impressive considering one of the teams, the Brewers, plays in MLB's smallest market. And they manhandled the Dodgers badly enough that ticket prices for Games 3 and 4 fell at Dodger Stadium.

Fox said it was the most-watched Game 4 telecast on any network since 2018 and more than 7,300,000 fans were watching at peak audience.

Kurt has earned tremendous respect in our clubhouse, and I've seen firsthand how much he cares about our players. I do not believe our record this year was a true reflection of his abilities as a manager. I'm pleased we were able to offer Kurt a role to stay on as a special assistant, where his knowledge of our players and his perspective would continue to be valuable to the organization."

The Angels finished the 2026 season with a 62-100 record, missing the playoffs for the 12th consecutive year.

articles.title: Brewers Update $1000 'Timeless Ticket' Policy Ahead of World Series vs. Rays After Fan Criticism
articles.summary: The Milwaukee Brewers are offering a new promotion for fans unhappy with the seats they received for 2026 World Series games after redeeming a decade-old ticket promotion.
articles.body:
The Milwaukee Brewers are offering a new promotion for fans unhappy with the seats they received for 2026 World Series games after redeeming a decade-old ticket promotion.

The Brewers told fans in 2015 they could pay $1,000 for a "Timeless Ticket" while reportedly promising fans could redeem the ticket for the "best available seat" at any game in the future.

After complaints about the level of Fall Classic seats received through that promotion, the Brewers said Wednesday fans who had already redeemed their Timeless Ticket for a World Series game would be able to use the ticket again in the future.

"We heard feedback from some Timeless Ticket holders regarding the ticket redemption process and seating locations offered," the Brewers' email read (h/t Complex Sports).

The Brewers continued, "To ensure your Timeless Ticket receives the value originally intended... You will retain the World Series ticket you received this year, and your Timeless Ticket may still be redeemed for a future Brewers game in any future season."

The initial conditions of the Timeless Ticket promotion promised 1,000 fans a chance to buy a ticket that could be redeemed at "any single future Brewers game at Miller Park... whether it's Opening Day or the 7th game of the World Series."

The promotion stated the ticket "may be redeemed for the best available seat locations, subject to ticket availability at the time of redemption," per TMJ4 News' Ben Jordan.

The Brewers clinched the franchise's first trip to the World Series since 1982 by sweeping the Los Angeles Dodgers from the NLCS.

Brewers president of business operations Rick Schlesinger said days later the club "erred in our internal communications on the logistics of fulfilling the requests" to redeem Timeless Tickets, per the AP's Steve Megargee .

"While we were able to accommodate all with seats, we received feedback from some that they were unhappy with their seat locations," Schlesinger said. "Clearly, even with extraordinary limitations on available seats, we did not live up to the spirit of the program, and we have been working through a resolution."

Fans speaking with multiple reporters including Jordan and Megargee said the Brewers had responded to their requests to redeem the Timeless Ticket with offers for 400-level or standing-room only seats.

GameTime currently lists the get-in price in for Game 1 of the World Series in Milwaukee at more than $2,300. First pitch against the opening game against the Tampa Bay Rays is scheduled for Friday at 8 p.m. ET.

articles.title: Shohei Ohtani Injury Update, Pitching Status Revealed By Dodgers' Friedman After MLB Playoff Exit
articles.summary: Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Shohei Ohtani will not get surgery this offseason after left knee irritation and right biceps discomfort bothered him for much of the 2026 campaign, per Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman at the end-of-year press conference.
articles.body:
Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Shohei Ohtani will not get surgery this offseason after left knee irritation and right biceps discomfort bothered him for much of the 2026 campaign, per Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman at the end-of-year press conference.

The GM also noted that he expects the four-time MVP to pitch next season.

Over the 2023-2025 seasons, Ohtani averaged 51 home runs and 109 RBI. He posted a .298 batting average and 1.037 OPS. He won MVP awards all three seasons (American League in 2023, when he played for the Los Angeles Angels).

However, Ohtani dealt with injuries from for much of 2026 and through the playoffs, and his numbers dipped (30 homers, 81 RBI, .275 average, .889 OPS). Those are still great numbers overall, and he was in the NL MVP conversation this season.

Ohtani started the year great on the pitcher's mound, going 8-2 with a 1.79 ERA (0.95 WHIP) and 95 strikeouts in 14 starts. However, Ohtani made his last start of the season on July 3 after exiting with right biceps tightness.

Over his final 18 regular season games, Ohtani hit .157 (.503 OPS). He had no home runs and just one RBI. He went on the 15-day injured list due to biceps and knee issues in September. The playoffs were a struggle as well, as Ohtani hit just .192 (.630 OPS) with 10 strikeouts in eight games.

L.A. won 100 games and reached the National League Championship Series but lost to the Milwaukee Brewers in a four-game sweep.

As far as the future goes, thankfully surgery is off the table for Ohtani, and an offseason of rest can certainly help as L.A. looks to rebound.

articles.title: Aaron Boone Defends Yankees Clubhouse Amid Accountability Criticism After MLB Playoff Exit
articles.summary: Fans in the Bronx and former players weren't thrilled with the 2026 version of the New York Yankees, with Hall of Famer CC Sabathia going so far as to say that the current players weren't living up to the "standard" expected of the organization.
articles.body:
Fans in the Bronx and former players weren't thrilled with the 2026 version of the New York Yankees, with Hall of Famer CC Sabathia going so far as to say that the current players weren't living up to the "standard" expected of the organization.

But manager Aaron Boone sees things a bit differently and defended the clubhouse culture on Wednesday.

"I think we can always be better at the standard because we expect to be a champion every year," he told reporters . "And I think we do have a lot of the right ingredients in that room that are pushing towards that standard. And I even look to our clubhouse this year, where I know that's been brought up... but I feel like our clubhouse this year was, again, a strength. This team dealt with a lot and handled it, and handled it without pointing fingers but just by sticking their nose down and competing really well."

Frustrations are understandable for an organization accustomed to winning—the Yankees haven't won a title since 2009, with the 17-year drought matching the team's longest in the modern era. But Boone doesn't believe the issue is stemming from the team's internal culture.

articles.title: Yankees Won't Be Sold Despite Recent $2.6B Financing Deal, Hal Steinbrenner Says
articles.summary: While the New York Yankees may have turned heads with a $2.6 billion financing deal from a private equity firm, team owner Hal Steinbrenner insisted it is not a signal the team will be sold in the coming years.
articles.body:
While the New York Yankees may have turned heads with a $2.6 billion financing deal from a private equity firm, team owner Hal Steinbrenner insisted it is not a signal the team will be sold in the coming years.

"It's not a precursor to fully selling the team," he said Wednesday when discussing the deal with Apollo Global Management, per Brendan Kuty of The Athletic. Instead, he said it was to provide "financial stability for years and years to come … including the year when I'm out of here and the third generation is running the team."

Last month, the New York Post reported the Yankees were valued at "significantly more than $12 billion" with the $2.6 billion cash injection, which is notable since the Los Angeles Lakers previously sold for a North American sports record at a $12.5 billion valuation.

Kuty reported the deal gives Apollo 16 percent ownership of the team, which comes in under the maximum amount of 20 percent that private equity is permitted to own according to MLB rules.

Despite the significance of the deal, Steinbrenner said Apollo has "zero" say in the team's daily operations and will "have rights no different than our other limited partners."

The valuation of the Yankees at such a high number could give Steinbrenner the opportunity to make a record profit if he did decide to sell the team in full, but his latest comments suggest he plans to keep it in the family for multiple generations.

Steinbrenner's father, George, purchased the Yankees in 1973 for $10 million, so the franchise has been in the family for more than 50 years.

New York has won seven World Series since 1973, although its most recent championship came 16 years ago in 2009. That may not seem like a long time for some franchises, but it is an eternity for the 27-ring Yankees.

They have come close of late having made the playoffs in nine of the last 10 years and the World Series in 2024, but this generation of pinstripes is yet to break through and reach MLB's mountaintop.

It seems like it will be up to the Steinbrenner family for the foreseeable future to put together a team that can change that.

articles.title: Shohei Ohtani expected to pitch next year; surgery 'not on the table'
articles.summary: Ohtani pitched in 14 games this year, taking the mound for the last time on July 3.
articles.body:
Los Angeles Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman spoke to reporters Wednesday and gave an update on star Shohei Ohtani.

Friedman said Ohtani dealt with knee and biceps injuries throughout the year and called the whole situation "whack-a-mole." Importantly, Friedman said surgery is "not on the table" for Ohtani, and he is expected to heal over the offseason.

The Dodgers are preparing for a full-strength, dual-threat Ohtani next year. Said Friedman: "I fully expect him to pitch next year. "

With the injuries, Ohtani played in 135 games this season. That ties for his fewest games played in a season since 2020. He took the mound 14 times, with his final pitching appearance on July 3, ahead of the All-Star break.

After hitting only in the second half, Ohtani was added to the injured list on Sept. 3 and wasn't activated until Sept. 29, as the Dodgers tried to give him extra time to rest before the postseason.

While he was active throughout L.A.'s playoff run, he wasn't himself at the plate. Ohtani played in eight postseason games and went 5-for-26. He slashed just .192/.323/.308 with one home run and three RBI.

Even with injuries affecting his play throughout the season, he was still very good. But Ohtani has set an unreal set of expectations for himself by winning three consecutive MVP awards.

In the 2026 regular season, he hit .275, his lowest batting average since 2022. He hit 30 home runs, his fewest since 2020.

The dual-threat star's numbers were down across the board, but he still helped Los Angeles to 100 wins, second-most in MLB. The Dodgers made the playoffs as the No. 2 seed in the National League. Los Angeles knocked off the Atlanta Braves in the NLDS, but the Milwaukee Brewers swept the Dodgers in the NLCS.

While Ohtani is expected to avoid surgery, the same isn't true for Los Angeles catcher Dalton Rushing. LA Times writer Maddie Lee reported Wednesday that the catcher will undergo right elbow surgery.

Rushing is expected to undergo a "hybrid internal brace procedure" that will sideline him from catching for nine months, though Lee says he's expected to be hitting well before then.
