articles.title: 10 things to know about the Rays before they play for their first World Series title
articles.summary: The 2026 World Series is guaranteed a first-time champion. It could very well be the AL champion Rays.
articles.body:
For the first time in four-and-a-half decades, the 2026 World Series is guaranteed to result in a first-time champion. It could very well be the American League champion Tampa Bay Rays.

After a six-game win over the Cleveland Guardians in the ALCS , the Rays are set to face the NL champion Milwaukee Brewers in the Fall Classic . It is the first time since the 1980 World Series between the Philadelphia Phillies and Kansas City Royals that two teams without titles have faced each other.

Game 1 is scheduled for 8 p.m. ET Friday in Milwaukee .

The World Series features two undeniably small-market teams, but both have been punching above their weight class for years. We already talked about how the Brewers have done this , so let's dive into how the Rays operate.

They are the classic small-payroll, big-brain team

No team in MLB exemplifies the sort of club that overcomes a lack of payroll with smart decisions like the Rays. They are the shorthand for that archetype, and 2026 has become a strong example of why.

The Rays rank 28th in MLB payroll this season, at $90 million, per RosterResource . They are the third-cheapest team in MLB, ahead of only their ALCS foe Guardians ($87 million) and the Miami Marlins ($76 million). Even the Brewers are well ahead of the Rays at 19th ($142 million).

Whichever team wins will be the cheapest World Series champion since at least the 2017 Houston Astros (cue snickering), but the Rays would introduce an entirely different degree of rarity. Going off data from Cot's Contracts , the last World Series winner with a sub-$100 million year-end 40-man payroll was the 2006 St. Louis Cardinals at $91 million, which ranked 10th in MLB at the time.

This entire decade has seemingly operated on the rule that you need a big payroll to win a title. The Rays would completely undercut that.

This is their third chance at a first World Series

Unlike the Brewers, who are returning to the World Series for the first time since 1982, the Rays aren't decades removed from the World Series.

Tampa Bay has reached the Fall Classic twice, in 2008 and 2020. It lost the former to the Philadelphia Phillies and the latter to the Los Angeles Dodgers.

This current Rays roster doesn't bring much experience from those series. On the Rays' ALCS roster, only designated hitter Yandy Díaz was part of that 2020 team. The rest of the team has completely turned over (save for injured ace Shane McClanahan).

MLB fans over 30 likely remember a time when the expansion team in Tampa Bay was a laughingstock, trapped in a division featuring the New York Yankees and Boston Red Sox. The Rays began their existence with nine last-place finishes in 10 years, with the only exception being a fourth-place finish in 2004. Their first World Series appearance in 2008 also happened to be their first winning season.

The moment everything changed can be traced back to 2003, when team owner Stuart Sternberg met a college baseball player-turned-finance guy by the name of Andrew Friedman. By 2005, Friedman was general manager and leading the front office to a new frontier of analytics. Friedman left Tampa Bay in 2014 to do something similar with vastly more resources for the Los Angeles Dodgers, but the Rays have kept plugging on without him under current president of baseball operations Erik Neander.

Like an NFL coaching tree, so many successful GMs in today's game can trace their lineage back to the Rays under Friedman and Neander. That includes Brewers president of baseball operations Matt Arnold, who worked under Friedman in Tampa from 2007 until his departure in 2015.

It can't be denied that Tampa Bay's fortunes have ebbed and flowed under this direction — the team won only 77 games last year — but few teams have been better at staying one step ahead of the competition from an ideas perspective. For the Rays, that's a matter of survival.

As for the manager side, Kevin Cash is MLB's longest-tenured manager, having taken over the dugout in 2015 in the aftermath of Friedman's departure (which triggered manager Joe Maddon's departure). Clearly, the front office appreciates his ability to implement its ideas.

They've been the AL's best team all season

In a chaotic AL season featuring division champions with 85 wins and 81 wins, the Rays stood out as the league's only truly elite team at 98-64. That has borne out in the playoffs as well.

A fun quirk of the MLB playoff structure meant the Rays had to start their postseason against the AL's second-winningest team, the 93-win New York Yankees. They swept them in the ALDS. Then came the Guardians, who at least made it a series at 2-2 before the Rays pulled away in Games 5 and 6.

As is the case with the Brewers, it really shouldn't be a surprise that Tampa Bay is here. This is a true No. 1 vs. No. 1 matchup .

It's a common criticism of modern baseball that hitters strike out too much, though much of that can be blamed on the unreasonable challenge of facing modern pitching velocity.

Consider the Rays a throwback in this regard. No team in MLB struck out at a lower clip than Tampa Bay at 18.8%, which helped the club post the best batting average in the AL at .258.

Not a single member of this team struck out more than 25% in the regular season (min. 200 plate appearances). By comparison, the Brewers have four such players. The Rays prioritize making contact, even if it's not always good contact, as they ranked third-lowest in both hard-hit rate and line-drive rate during the regular season, per FanGraphs.

That makes for an interesting comparison with the Brewers, who swing less than any team in MLB and led the league in walk rate. The Rays actually rank in the middle of the pack when it comes to how much they swing, but no team in MLB makes contact more frequently when they do swing .

Neither approach leads to a ton of home runs — the Rays ranked 22nd in MLB this season, the Brewers tied for 28th — but it speaks to how intentionally these two teams have been crafted. Both are the best in the sport when it comes to two very important components of hitting: making contact and patience at the plate.

Not many people are going to be describing Díaz, Jonathan Aranda and Junior Caminero as the faces of MLB, but those three have formed Tampa Bay's offensive backbone this season. And all three had big moments in the ALCS.

Díaz has long been an ultra-patient hitter, and he led the AL in hits this season. He has flexed his muscle in the postseason with six extra-base hits, one of them a game-sealing homer in Game 6 against the Guardians .

Aranda broke out as an All-Star last year but went hitless in his first 11 ALCS at-bats. However, he either hit or scored on the three biggest plays of Game 4, which swung the series back in the Rays' favor.

Caminero was a homer short of leading the AL this season, with 42 to Pete Alonso's 43. The former elite prospect swings the bat harder than any player in baseball but still keeps the strikeouts under control, a rarity among modern power hitters. He was homerless for the entire postseason until Game 6, when he posted the longest home run trot on record in MLB postseason history.

The Rays' offense is actually pretty simple. Their first baseman, third baseman and designated hitter provide the wood. Everyone else can be counted on to at least deliver two-way value.

The effectiveness of team defense is often conveyed by number of errors or Gold Gloves, but ultimately, it comes down to how good a team is at turning balls in play into outs. That's what defensive efficiency measures, and the Rays are the best in the league .

The Rays' outfield — led by Jonny DeLuca, Chandler Simpson and Victor Mesa Jr. — led MLB in outs above average this season . Shortstop Taylor Walls is a Gold Glove finalist and the favorite to win the award. Ben Williamson can play any position in the infield well.

Between that group and the big three hitters, odds are that every Rays position player is going to be very good to elite in at least one important thing. That includes baserunning.

Since he made his MLB debut last season, no player has more stolen bases than Simpson's 90. To be fair, no player has been caught stealing more times than his 26, but he's 3-for-3 this postseason, and his speed on the basepaths has definitely factored into games.

Simpson also led the AL in bunt hits, with teammates Cedric Mullins and Walls right behind him. Again, the Rays want to make contact, and they're happy to use their speed to make up for any loss in power.

Funnily enough, it's the Rays and Brewers who have embraced the bunt more than any other teams in MLB. The Rays led MLB in both bunt hits ( 49 ) and sacrifice bunts (45) this season, while the Brewers ranked second (32) and fifth (37) in those areas.

For all that's made about bunting being anathema for the analytics-minded, these are two analytics-heavy teams trying to zig where the rest of the industry has zagged.

Former All-Star starter Shane McClanahan was shut down earlier this month due to forearm tightness . That's a huge loss for the Rays, but the team has made do with a postseason rotation of Drew Rasmussen, Freddy Peralta, Nick Martinez and Griffin Jax.

Rasmussen is the staff ace, but Peralta has been just as important this postseason . The former Brewers pitcher was traded from Milwaukee to the New York Mets last offseason and was an outright disaster in Queens, posting a 4.99 ERA in 22 starts. He was sent to the Rays at the trade deadline and has since morphed back into a standout starting pitcher.

Peralta won AL Pitcher of the Month honors in September and has pitched in four straight wins for the Rays since the postseason began, with a 1.08 ERA. In the span of three months, he has salvaged a contract season.

How did the Rays do it? You can read more here , but the game plan includes ditching the wind-up and pitching out of the stretch, moving his foot placement on the rubber, throwing his changeup more and speeding up his delivery. That is a lot of changes, but the result has been a pitcher who is once again dominating with his fastball.

Unlike the Brewers, the Rays are willing to ride their starting pitcher into the later innings if possible. Part of that is a reflection of their strong rotation, but it might also be a sign of a bullpen that has only so many arms you can trust.

Bryan Baker is this team's closer. Cam Booser has been brilliant from the left side this postseason. Tyler Wells and Ian Seymour were effective setup men during the regular season, but both had multiple ugly outings in the ALCS.

Beyond that group, no reliever has thrown more than three innings across Tampa Bay's nine postseason games. The Rays went as far as using Peralta for two outs in relief in Game 4 of the ALCS.

That might be as close to a weakness as the Brewers are going to find with this Tampa Bay roster. The Rays can afford only so many short starts from their rotation, and they are facing a Milwaukee team that is the best in baseball at pestering starters out of the game, as we saw them do against the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS.

articles.title: Rays vs. Brewers 2026 World Series Picks and Player Predictions in MLB Postseason
articles.summary: The 2026 World Series is going to make history. Either the Tampa Bay Rays or Milwaukee Brewers are about to claim their first championship.
articles.body:
The 2026 World Series is going to make history. Either the Tampa Bay Rays or Milwaukee Brewers are about to claim their first championship.

So, that's what's at stake. But what should everyone expect?

According to FanDuel , the Brewers are the favorite (-172) and the Rays are the underdog (+148). Yet this is ultimately a 103-win team against a 98-win team, and both clubs play a very similar style of baseball.

It's therefore worth getting in depth with the specifics of this matchup before making any predictions. Who are the key players? What are the key matchups? What are the X-factors that will determine the series?

Let's see what we can see, and then we'll present picks for the winner of the World Series and for the World Series MVP.

Game 1 (Friday, October 23): Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8:00 p.m. ET

Game 2 (Saturday, October 24): Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8:00 p.m. ET

Game 3 (Monday, October 26): Milwaukee at Tampa Bay, 8:00 p.m. ET

Game 4 (Tuesday, October 27): Milwaukee at Tampa Bay, 8:00 p.m. ET

Game 5 (Wednesday, October 28)*: Milwaukee at Tampa Bay, 8:00 p.m. ET

Game 6 (Friday, October 30)*: Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8:00 p.m. ET

Game 7 (Saturday, October 31)*: Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8:00 p.m. ET

Caminero has been the driving force in the Rays' lineup over the last two seasons, slamming over 40 home runs and racking up over 100 RBI in each. Yet he went cool with a season-low .772 OPS in September, and he initially struggled to snap out of it once the postseason began.

That changed in the last three games of the ALCS. The 23-year-old had hits in all three, including a home run in the clincher that he soaked in as much as possible ( and then some ). Is he back? It sure seems like he's back.

Even if he's not as big of a power threat as Caminero, Díaz rarely fails to have a good at-bat or to hit the ball on a line. He's hit an even .300 across the last four seasons, and he led the AL in hits this year.

The 35-year-old was not the MVP of the ALCS, but he could have been. He torched the Cleveland Guardians for a 1.061 OPS and six extra-base hits, culminating in the two-run homer that iced Game 6.

Even if he didn't get a ton of hype, Rasmussen was a ball-knower's ace in the regular season between 2022 and 2026. He posted a sub-3.00 ERA annually, and he even led the AL in WHIP this season.

Now the secret is out. The 31-year-old's three starts in the playoffs have yielded just three earned runs in 21.0 innings, with 23 strikeouts and only three walks. His changeup has been especially lethal, holding hitters to three hits in 24 at-bats.

Peralta was with the Brewers this time last year, and his journey since then has taken him to lows with the New York Mets and now highs again with the Rays. He's coming into the World Series hot off being named the ALCS MVP.

The 30-year-old doesn't offer a complicated scouting report. He's throwing his fastball about 70 percent of the time in October, daring hitters to beat him on his best pitch. They haven't, going just 8-for-39 against it so far.

Baker blew his third save of the year back on May 13. He hasn't blown one since in 53 turns on the mound, along the way allowing just five earned runs in 52.0 innings.

The 31-year-old's velocity has declined throughout the year, but that has yet to translate into any kind of advantage for hitters. It could be because he uses his fastball and changeup in roughly equal tandem, using both to hold hitters to one hit in 21 at-bats thus far in October.

The Brewers signed Chourio to an $84 million contract before he had played even one game in the majors. It has paid off in the form of three straight 20-20 seasons, and all before he's turned even 23 years old.

On paper, his .171 batting average and .553 OPS say he's not having a good postseason. Yet even if the Brewers would like more consistency, they'll take the clutch gene that has delivered seven RBI, including two that snatched victory from the jaws of defeat.

There were 137 players who took at least 500 plate appearances this season, and only 12 of them had a better OPS+ than Bauers. Not bad for a 31-year-old who had an 84 OPS+ for his career coming into the season.

Bauers has become a menace of another sort in the playoffs. Even if he only has one multi-hit game, he's shown tremendous patience in racking up a .441 OBP and driving in six runs. He had multiple at-bats that dug the Los Angeles Dodgers' grave as he was winning MVP honors for the NLCS.

Contreras has regressed a little as a regular-season performer, but you'd never know from how he's hit this postseason. He's hit safely in six of eight games, with three home runs and five RBI.

Also, don't overlook his mastery of the ABS. He challenged a league-high 185 calls from behind the plate this season, and he won 80 of them. He's kept it up in the playoffs, going 8-for-12 and winning some truly game-changing challenges.

After making 30 starts and pitching to a 1.80 ERA and a 5.7 K/BB ratio, Misiorowski is going to win the NL Cy Young Award. As soon as he hit 104.8 mph on his first pitch of the playoffs, he seemed ready to tap into still another gear for October.

Except, he hasn't made it past the fifth inning in either of his two assignments, consisting of nine hits and four walks in 8.1 total innings. He clearly isn't gassed, but he'll need to be better to maximize Milwaukee's chances in the World Series.

Milwaukee's entire bullpen has been incredible in the playoffs, handling 40.2 innings and allowing just six earned runs. Trevor Megill and Abner Uribe deserve their flowers, too.

Yet Ashby has simply been on another level, thus far posting 12.1 shutout innings and allowing just four hits and three walks. The next hitter who gets a knock off his curveball, changeup or slider will be the first.

Matchups That Will Define the World Series

Junior Caminero's Bat Speed vs. the Brewers' Velocity

What makes Caminero so dangerous? For one thing, nobody whips the bat through the zone like he does. His average swing this season was 79.5 mph, the highest of any qualified hitter.

In the World Series, though, he'll be up against a Brewers pitching staff that is averaging 98.3 mph on the fastball. That's almost a full mile per hour faster than the hardest-throwing staff of the 2025 playoffs.

Chandler Simpson's Speed vs. the Brewers' Defenders

Simpson is basically a free 90 feet in human form. He had 11 more infield hits than anyone else this season. He also stole 46 bases, and took 21 more bases on wild pitches, passed balls and the like. It all makes him a rare weapon.

The Brewers, though, could be up to stopping him. Their infield was among the very best this season with a total output of +7 Outs Above Average. More to the point, William Contreras was second in the league in caught-stealings.

Jacob Misiorowski vs. the Rays' High-Contact Offense

Misiorowski's contact rate during the regular season was a mere 65.5 percent, easily the best in baseball. Yet he hasn't been nearly as successful at avoiding contact in the postseason, where his rate has jumped to 77.4 percent.

If the San Diego Padres and Los Angeles Dodgers could do that, the Rays should be able to as well. They led MLB with an 81.8 contact percentage during the regular season, and it has only gone down to 77.2 in the postseason.

The Brewers' Lefty Bats vs. the Rays' Righty-Heavy Pitching

It isn't just Jake Bauers. Milwaukee's left-handed hitters as a collective have a 122 wRC+ in the playoffs, and that's despite facing some darn good left-handed pitching. In the NLCS alone, they faced a pair of two-time Cy Young Award winners in Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell.

The Rays aren't nearly as synonymous with left-handed pitching, indeed carrying only three for the ALCS against Cleveland. And one of them (Ian Seymour) isn't looking so hot after carrying a heavy workload in the regular season.

X-Factors That Will Define the World Series

The best home record in MLB during the regular season? Well, it was a tie at 55-26… between the Rays and Brewers, naturally.

Neither club has fumbled its home-field advantage in the postseason. The Brewers are 4-0 at American Family Field. The Rays are 4-1 at Tropicana Field. So on paper, both teams can claim to have an advantage on their home turf.

That said, it's the Brewers who truly stand to find out. If this series goes the distance, they'll have the honor of hosting the finale in Milwaukee on October 31.

For the uninitiated, the three true outcomes are strikeouts, walks and home runs. Neither the Rays nor the Brewers was necessarily synonymous with the concept during the regular season, specifically in the sense that they both ranked in the bottom 10 of the league in home runs.

They have since gone on wildly different paths in October. The Brewers' percentage of three true outcomes when on offense is at 47 percent. For the Rays, it's only 31 percent.

Both paths have ultimately arrived in the same spot, but this may be where we find out which one wins the day. Can the Brewers keep winning by racking up walks and homers? Or, will the Rays avoid enough strikeouts to gain the inside track?

Regardless of what happens in the TTO department, neither of these teams should be expected to give much away, while both should be expected to take as much as they can get.

In other words, they're both good at fielding the ball and running the bases. The Rays and Brewers each ranked in the top six for defensive efficiency this season. They were both top-five in stolen bases, and separated by just two steals in the end.

In these respects, the World Series should reward baseball purists for their attention. The result could come down to fine margins—a ball just out of reach or a tag applied just in time.

Predicting the Outcome and World Series MVP

Regarding my credentials, I had the Brewers sweeping the Dodgers in the NLCS before it happened . So, I've been right at least once in my life.

Yet whereas the Dodgers looked old, slow and generally out of sorts while trying to keep pace with Milwaukee, the Rays are cut from the same cloth as a ballclub. They're younger and more athletic, and committed to playing smart, clean baseball that emphasizes the little things to add up to one big haymaker.

One area where Milwaukee should have an edge is on offense. The Brewers have as many as five hitters you really have to worry about. The Rays really only have three, in Junior Caminero, Yandy Díaz and Jonathan Aranda.

The Brewers' bullpen stands out as another advantage, even if they'll need more from their starters to avoid their relievers getting overexposed in a longer series. It, too, is deeper than what the Rays have to offer. And let's be real that Milwaukee relievers are simply on a heater right now.

So, congratulations in advance to the Brewers. If anything is worth a 57-year wait, it's a World Series championship.

This pick is partially about deferring to a hot hand. The Brewers have gotten contributions from all their hitters in the postseason, but Contreras has been a constant the whole way through. You just can't fake a 1.157 OPS.

Between his ABS challenges and his ability to control the running game, Contreras' defense also stands to be a huge factor in the World Series. He could also be a not-so-secret weapon when Freddy Peralta pitches for the Rays. If anyone knows him, it's the guy who caught him 81 times between 2023 and 2025.

Stats courtesy of Baseball Reference , FanGraphs and Baseball Savant .

articles.title: Tarik Skubal and the Next 10 Players to Sign $200 Million Contracts
articles.summary: Assuming something resembling a normal MLB offseason emerges from the rubble of CBA negotiations this winter, two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal could be in line for a record-setting payday for a pitcher.
articles.body:
Assuming something resembling a normal MLB offseason emerges from the rubble of CBA negotiations this winter, two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal could be in line for a record-setting payday for a pitcher.

At the very least, he's a lock to exceed $200 million in his first trip to free agency. He could be eyeing a $400 million mega deal as one of the best pitchers to ever hit the open market.

There is a steep drop-off in earning power behind him in this year's free-agent class, but there are high-profile extension candidates across baseball, and more and more teams are making an early push to lock up young talent.

Ahead, we've taken a shot at predicting the next 10 players who will sign $200 million contracts, with age, production, long-term outlook and proximity to free agency all factors in building the list.

Contract Status: Arbitration-eligible through 2028

Whether he is the centerpiece of a blockbuster deal or a foundational building block for the Nationals, CJ Abrams has put himself in position for a massive payday following a career year offensively.

Still only 26 years old, he posted a 127 OPS+ with 30 doubles, 33 home runs, 106 RBI and 34 steals in a 5.1-WAR season, earning his second All-Star selection in the last three years.

Despite his defensive shortcomings and a potential long-term move to second base, his age and offensive impact make him an obvious candidate for a lucrative extension and the potential headliner of the 2028-29 free-agent class.

Even as a second baseman, he will have a strong case to eclipse the seven-year, $175 million deal that Marcus Semien signed with the Rangers prior to his age-31 season.

Contract Status: Two years, $53.7 million remaining on contract

Teams buying out the final year or two of a superstar's contract to lock him up with a fresh long-term extension is common practice. No one is a more obvious candidate for that approach than presumptive AL MVP Yordan Alvarez.

With two years remaining on his six-year, $115 million extension, and fresh off a season where he hit .316/.432/.601 with 42 home runs and 106 RBI to make a run at AL Triple Crown honors, he is unquestionably one of the game's elite offensive talents.

His back-loaded current deal will pay him $26.8 million in 2027 and 2028, so replacing those two years with a fresh long-term deal and an AAV somewhere in the $30 million range would not actually be tacking that much onto the payroll next year.

The Astros could also decide it's time to rebuild, which would make him a blockbuster trade chip and an obvious extension candidate for any team that ponies up the prospect talent to land him.

Contract Status: Pre-arbitration, controllable through 2030

Junior Caminero will not reach arbitration for the first time until after the 2027 season. At that point, he might be in line for a record-setting payday if he continues to produce at the level he has in the last two seasons.

2025: 154 G, 130 OPS+, 45 HR, 110 RBI, 4.3 WAR 2026: 162 G, 144 OPS+, 42 HR, 101 RBI, 5.7 WAR

The Rays have never signed a player to a contract worth a guaranteed $200 million, but Caminero is a face-of-the-franchise caliber superstar worth committing a significant chunk of the payroll to for the foreseeable future.

The additional revenue that will come from their World Series trip, coupled with the potential for a salary floor to be instituted in the upcoming CBA negotiations, raises the chances of Caminero inking an extension.

The 11-year, $288.8 million extension Bobby Witt Jr. signed with the Royals is a reasonable starting point in negotiations, but we are inching closer to Vladimir Guerrero Jr.'s 14-year, $500 million deal with every ball he sends into the seats.

A Possible Trade Made by Every Team This Offseason ⚾

Contract Status: Arbitration-eligible through 2029

The Reds have already approached Elly De La Cruz with an extension offer.

"We engaged in Spring Training of 2025 and presented an offer," Reds president of baseball operations Nick Krall told reporters in January. "The offer would have been the largest contract in Reds history. We didn't have any further conversations regarding the offer."

The current largest contract in club history is the 10-year, $225 million deal Joey Votto signed in 2012, so he has already had the opportunity to join the $200 million club and declined.

With Scott Boras as his agent and coming off the best season of his career, in which he showed improved defensive chops alongside his tantalizing power-speed combination, the likelihood of him signing an early extension is extremely low.

The Reds could eventually put him on the trade block if an extension doesn't work out. Any team acquiring him would likely want to get a long-term deal on the books. That provides multiple avenues for a huge payday in the coming years.

Contract Status: Arbitration-eligible through 2027

The volatility of pitchers makes mega contracts far less common, though Dylan Cease did reel in a seven-year, $210 million payday from the Blue Jays last offseason, even coming off an inconsistent contract year.

Over the last five seasons, Logan Gilbert has averaged 31 starts and 180.1 innings while posting a 3.46 ERA and 110 ERA+. That durability and consistency make him a prime candidate for a massive contract.

His 14.2 WAR over that five-year stretch ranks among the top 20 among all pitchers. Whether it's an extension from the Mariners or as the top arm in the 2027-28 free-agent class, a boatload of money is on the horizon.

The 29-year-old played on a $10.9 million salary last season. He is projected to earn $15.4 million in his final year of arbitration, which would make him an extremely attractive trade chip if Seattle decided to deal from its pitching depth.

In a down year by his own lofty standards, Gunnar Henderson was still a 3.2-WAR player, posting a 102 OPS+ with 57 extra-base hits and 24 home runs while starting 149 games at shortstop.

After a 6.1-WAR rookie season in 2023 and an 8.8-WAR follow-up season in which he finished fourth in AL MVP voting, he firmly established himself as one of the game's brightest young stars.

He looked like a clear long-term building block while the Orioles were on the rise, but their stalled progress toward contention led to the Adley Rutschman trade this past summer. That might not be the end of the roster turnover.

MLB insider Buster Olney made headlines in August when he said, "he's not going to sign there long term in all likelihood," while discussing Henderson's future. Whether he is the next homegrown star out the door or reaches free agency after the 2028 season, he will command big money.

Contract Status: One year, $17.5 million remaining on contract

Despite a prolific run in the Japanese League, Munetaka Murakami was not met with the robust market many expected last offseason due to swing-and-miss concerns. He signed a two-year, $34 million deal with the White Sox. That translated into him becoming the center of their surprising climb to the postseason.

The 26-year-old had a .207 batting average and 35.4 percent strikeout rate, but his on-base ability (16.6 BB%, .347 OBP) and power (130 OPS+, 35 HR) still made him one of the most impactful sluggers in baseball.

If he can match that performance in his second season stateside, a significantly more lucrative contract likely awaits in his next trip to free agency.

Pete Alonso got a $31 million AAV on a five-year deal ahead of his age-31 season as an elite power hitter with limited secondary value. Murakami will be four years younger when he shops for his next contract. Even if he doesn't match that AAV, a longer deal could easily push the full value above $200 million.

At first glance, Jeremy Peña is not an obvious candidate for a $200 million deal, but never underestimate the earning power of a quality shortstop in a thin market at the position.

The 29-year-old has taken his offensive game to another level the past two seasons, logging a .291/.345/.477 line and 130 OPS+ despite missing some time to injuries. He remains a standout defender.

With 22.2 WAR over his first five seasons and a playoff track record few players his age can match, he would be an obvious extension candidate if not for the fact that he switched agents and hired Scott Boras in June 2025.

That clearly indicates he intends to test the market after the 2027 season, which could put him on the trade block this winter. Xander Bogaerts was the same age when he signed his 11-year, $280 million contract with the Padres. While he had a longer track record, Peña is a far superior defender.

Tarik Skubal was the only 2026-27 free agent projected to earn a contract north of $200 million in my recent article predicting the 10 biggest contracts handed out in free agency this winter.

The nine-year, $324 million contract that Gerrit Cole signed prior to the 2020 season is a logical starting point, but Skubal could be aiming for a $40 million AAV given his track record and the rising cost of frontline pitching.

Barring a surprise mega-deal for Japanese League star Teruaki Sato, the odds are extremely high that Skubal will be the next free agent to lock in at least $200 million.

With a 2.42 ERA, 0.92 WHIP and 655 strikeouts in 546 innings over the last three seasons, he has firmly established himself as one of the best pitchers in the sport in the prime of his career.

Contract Status: Arbitration-eligible through 2030

One of the key return pieces from the Juan Soto blockbuster trade with the Padres, James Wood has developed into one of the best young sluggers in baseball and the face of the franchise for the Nationals.

The towering 6'6" outfielder has put together consecutive 30-homer, 3-WAR seasons. This year, he quietly developed into a more complete hitter beneath the surface of his 144 OPS+ and 30 long balls.

The 24-year-old raised his walk rate (12.3 to 16.4 percent), lowered his strikeout rate (32.1 to 28.7 percent) and added 21 steals in 25 attempts without sacrificing any of his power production.

After signing Cade Cavalli to a four-year, $47 million extension in September, the Nationals could be looking to lock up more pieces this offseason. Wood is the top candidate for a franchise cornerstone-level deal.

articles.title: Cardinals’ 5-Year Veteran Draws Interest From Astros
articles.summary: The St. Louis Cardinals’ World Series champion is among the names linked to a key opening with the Houston Astros.
articles.body:
The St. Louis Cardinals enter the offseason with reason to believe their rebuilding process is beginning to pay off.

Though they missed the playoffs this season, the organization has identified several young players who could form the foundation of its next competitive team. Now, the front office faces another challenge: continuing to develop that talent while making decisions that could shape the club's direction for years to come.

"The Cardinals overachieved in a rebuilding year and also learned who some of their long-term pieces are, from JJ Wetherholt to Jordan Walker to Joshua Baez to Leo Bernal," Will Leitch wrote for MLB.com . "This team will be contending, and likely soon. This offseason provides a fascinating opportunity, then."

While much of the attention will center on roster upgrades and player development, the Cardinals could also face an important question about its leadership group. One member of the organization's front office who is also a veteran of the team's pitching staff has reportedly attracted interest from a team looking to fill its own key executive position.

St Louis Cardinals Veteran Draws Houston Astros Interest

Cardinals assistant general manager Randy Flores is among the candidates who have drawn serious interest from the Houston Astros as they search for a new general manager.

"Longtime Milwaukee Brewers executive Matt Kleine, Chicago White Sox assistant general manager Josh Barfield, Kansas City Royals senior vice president Scott Sharp, Atlanta Braves assistant general manager Ben Sestanovich and St. Louis Cardinals assistant general manager Randy Flores are among the candidates who have drawn serious interest from the Astros," according to The Athletic's Chandler Rome .

Flores has a history with the Cardinals that extends beyond his current front-office role. The former southpaw pitched for the Cardinals from 2004 to 2008, winning a World Series with the team in 2006.

"Flores played in parts of eight major league seasons from 2002-10," Steve Adams wrote for MLB Trade Rumors . "The former ninth-round pick had a few strong seasons as a left-handed reliever, primarily for the same Cardinals that now employ him as an executive."

What St Louis Cardinals World Series Champion's Potential Houston Astros Move Could Mean

Flores' experience as both a former player and an executive should make him an appealing candidate for Houston. The Astros are seeking leadership for their baseball operations department, while Flores has been involved in the Cardinals' efforts to build a younger roster.

For St. Louis, losing an executive would potentially create another transition during a consequential phase of its rebuild. The organization has made progress identifying young players to build around, and its next steps will require continued evaluation of talent, player acquisition and long-term planning.

There is no indication in the cited report that Flores has been hired by Houston. His candidacy does, however, put the Cardinals' front office in the spotlight at a time when the franchise is trying to turn encouraging signs into sustained contention.

articles.title: MLB's new ABS challenge system could help decide 2026 World Series
articles.summary: Automatic Ball-Strike Challenge System rules remain in place for the World Series. Here's how effective the Brewers, Rays are with their challenges.
articles.body:
In the World Series , every moment is magnified. Even the umpires can feel immense pressure.

Any little mistake can tilt the balance of the Series, and remain with them for a lifetime .

Fortunately, MLB now has a video review system to minimize the impact of missed calls. In its first year of implementation at the major league level, the Automatic Ball-Strike (ABS) Challenge System seems to have been an overwhelming success.

While the number of replay challenges available for each manager increases from one to two in the playoffs, the ABS challenge rules are unchanged from the regular season. Each team begins the game with two challenges and keeps any challenges that are successful. If the game goes to extra innings, teams receive an additional challenge if they don't have any left at the start of an inning.

World Series champions through the years: See MLB's winners since 1996

Pitchers and catchers were generally more successful than batters in getting umpires' calls overturned during the 2026 regular season, according to Baseball Savant .

FIelders (catchers + pitchers): 3,358 of 5,792 (58%)

Interestingly, hitters for the two teams in this year's World Series, the Tampa Bay Rays and Milwaukee Brewers , had the worst results of any teams in the majors when challenging a strike call.

While their 46% success rate wasn't last overall, the runs above average they lost by challenging were the lowest in MLB. (Brewers -3.2 runs, Rays -3.9 runs)

Conversely, the two teams' pitchers and catchers were among the majors' most effective, with the Brewers gaining 2.2 runs above average (seventh overall) and the Rays gaining 1.6 (eighth).

In this year's postseason, those trends have continued − with hitters from the Brewers (-0.3 runs above average) and Rays (-1.1) ranking dead last among the 12 playoff teams, while their pitchers and catchers (Rays +0.6, Brewers +0.5) ranked first and second.

Brewers' strategy for challenging balls and strikes

Milwaukee manager Pat Murphy recently told USA TODAY Sports the Brewers have a rating system – 1 to 5 – regarding best and worst times to challenge, one they have refined for the playoffs.

"As long as you can identify what we call fives – good times to challenge, changing the at-bat," he says. "But do you change an at-bat with two outs, nobody on in the second inning? It's kind of identifying leverage and taking a chance there."

articles.title: MLB Free Agents 2026 Landing-Spot Predictions and Latest Rumors
articles.summary: While the Tampa Bay Rays and Milwaukee Brewers prepare to face off in the 2026 World Series, there are 28 other MLB teams making championship plans of their own.
articles.body:
While the Tampa Bay Rays and Milwaukee Brewers prepare to face off in the 2026 World Series, there are 28 other MLB teams making championship plans of their own.

It's just that their dreams won't be realized or dashed for at least another year.

Their offseason is on, and they need to use it fortify their roster for what they hope will be deep playoff runs. Some may materialize as soon as next season. Others could be looking much farther ahead.

Either way, they have rosters to upgrade, and there are free agents capable of providing that lift. Let's break down the latest buzz surrounding some of the top players on the market.

Michael King Eyeing Return to East Coast?

If San Diego Padres ace Michael King wants to be part of this free agent class, it'll cost him. He holds player options for the next two seasons totaling $58 million, meaning he'd have to decline that money to reach the open market.

And he might actually want to do that. He just posted a strong 3.21 ERA over a career-high 185 innings, so locking on a lock-term contract now might be best for his future.

He should have a host of suitors awaiting his decision, but if he "doesn't stay in San Diego, he may prefer options on the East Coast," per The Athletic's Patrick Mooney and Sahadev Sharma . "He went to high school in Rhode Island, played at Boston College and excelled as a swingman for the New York Yankees."

Of course, maybe the most important part of this discussion is the very start—the possibility of simply staying in San Diego. He has talked about having "a second home on the West Coast" now, and it sure sounds like he isn't in a rush to leave.

Prediction: King opts out and re-signs with the San Diego Padres.

Tigers Unlikely to Win Bidding War for Tarik Skubal?

The Detroit Tigers have seen Tarik Skubal at his absolute best. In fact, they've had a closer look at his superstar ascension than anyone.

They took him in the ninth round of the 2018 draft and then helped foster his rise into a two-time AL Cy Young winner. They were the only MLB employer he'd known until August, when they made the difficult decision to trade him away for assets and avoid risking him leaving in free agency for nothing.

But just as soon as he'd left, he opened the door to a possible return . The Tigers would surely love to make this happen, but they'll need his help. As MLB.com's Mark Feinsand noted, "it seems unlikely that the Tigers will get involved in a bidding war," so they'd need Skubal's decision to come down to something other than collecting the most cash.

While free agents do consider factors behind their pay day, the dollar amounts typically need to be pretty close to garner serious consideration. And with a bidding war seemingly brewing between the deep-pocketed Los Angeles Dodgers and New York Mets, the Tigers could get priced out of this sweepstakes.

Prediction: Skubal re-signs with the Los Angeles Dodgers.

OK, so you caught us—this is trade talk, not free agency buzz. But with the free agent class largely underwhelming, it makes sense to widen the lens, particularly when it comes to a prominent World Series participant perhaps being moved over the offseason.

That participant is Brewers catcher William Contreras, who secured his third All-Star selection this season. He has one of the best bats at the position (.275 average with 75 homers and 340 RBI over the past four seasons), which normally would make him someone Milwaukee clearly has to keep, but the business of baseball might get in the way.

"Contreras will be entering the last year of his deal in 2027, and with so many teams needing catching, he will surely draw trade interest," FanSided's Robert Murray wrote. "Right now, with the Brewers reaching the World Series, they are not thinking about such a scenario. But other teams are surely monitoring the situation, and it would be very easy to see a team such as, say, the New York Yankees calling to see what it would take to acquire Contreras."

Trading Contreras wouldn't help the Brewers now (or maybe any time soon), but it might be what's best for the franchise's future. If they aren't prepared to pay what it'll cost to keep him next offseason, then moving him during this one could be the best option on the board.

Prediction: Contreras is traded to the New York Yankees.

articles.title: How Brewers and Rays will make World Series MLB history not seen since 1980
articles.summary: This World Series matchup is something MLB hasn't seen in over 45 years.
articles.body:
The Milwaukee Brewers have made the 2026 MLB World Series, beating the Los Angeles Dodgers in a four-game sweep in the NLCS. The Tampa Bay Rays , after winning in six games in the ALCS over the Cleveland Guardians , are their opponent.

This is a fun matchup for neutral fans, but especially for Brewers and Rays fans. The reason why? Neither team has won a World Series before. This season, there will be a first-time World Series-winning club. That's a very cool feat on the horizon.

ESPN's David Schoenfield revealed that this fun World Series matchup is actually making MLB history that hasn't been seen since 1980. How? Well, that World Series 46 years ago was the last time two teams faced off that had never won a title before.

Brewers and Rays make World Series history not seen in 46 years

"The Brewers are in their 57th season in Milwaukee. The Rays are in their 29th season in Tampa Bay. Neither franchise has won a World Series," Schoenfield writes. "The last time this kind of World Series matchup was in 1980, when the Philadelphia Phillies beat the Kansas City Royals ."

Just like the Philadelphia Phillies and Kansas City Royals 46 years ago, the 2026 Brewers and Rays will guarantee that a franchise that has never won a World Series title will get their first this season.

While there's been some really fun matchups over the years, including back in 2016 when Cleveland and the Chicago Cubs faced off, this is the first time in quite a while that both teams hadn't ever won a World Series before.

There's been longer droughts in MLB history, with the Cubs and Cleveland Guardians having a ridiculous 174 combined seasons without a title.

This year's matchup "comes as the seventh-longest combined drought World Series," according to Schoenfield, with their 85 combined seasons without a title two seasons behind the Phillies and Royals back in 1980.

While these are two newer franchises in the grand scheme of MLB history, they both have never won a title before, which guarantees one fanbase will celebrate a title for the first time since the franchise was created.

That alone is reason enough to tune in, but with both of these teams being No. 1 seeds in the AL and NL, this is the kind of matchup that could be an all-time incredible World Series. The Brewers vs. Rays World Series begins Friday, and it should be a great one.

articles.title: World Series 2026: It will be Jacob Misiorowski vs. Nick Martinez in Game 1 as Brewers host Rays
articles.summary: Game 1 of the World Series begins at 8 p.m. ET Friday in Milwaukee.
articles.body:
The Milwaukee Brewers will have Jacob Misiorowski go up against Nick Martinez of the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 1 of the 2026 World Series on Friday at American Family Field.

Misiorowski, who led all MLB pitchers during the regular season with 252 strikeouts, will make his third start this postseason after throwing four innings and 4 1/3 innings against the San Diego Padres and Los Angeles Dodgers, respectively. Despite his mediocre performance by his standards, both starts resulted in the Brewers taking 1-0 leads in the NLDS and NLCS.

During Game 1 of the NLDS against the Padres, the Brewers' ace's first pitch was clocked at 104.8 mph, the fastest in the playoffs since MLB started tracking pitch speeds.

Misiorowski, 24, will be well rested for Friday, as he will have had 11 days off since his last trip to the mound. This will be the Brewers' first World Series appearance since 1982 and only the second in franchise history.

Martinez, 36, will be making his 11th career postseason start and third in these playoffs. He pitched 3 2/3 innings in Game 3 of the ALDS against the Yankees and allowed two runs on five hits. He next threw in Game 4 of the ALCS against the Guardians, going 5 1/3 innings with one earned run and two hits allowed. Both ended with important road victories for the Rays.

Martinez has been more productive away from Tropicana Field this season. His ERA at home during the regular season was 3.90, compared to 2.43 on the road, which includes the playoffs.

For Tampa Bay, Drew Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta are expected to take the ball for Games 2 and 3. The Brewers' pitching plans are not yet known, though Logan Henderson is the likely Game 2 starter.

This postseason, Rasmussen has recorded 23 strikeouts in 21 innings with a 0.76 WHIP while holding opponents to a .178 batting average. ALCS MVP Peralta has recorded a 0.90 ERA with 39 strikeouts over his past nine starts.

Game 1 of the 2026 World Series between the Rays and Brewers begins at 8 p.m. ET Friday on Fox, Fox One and Fox Deportes.

articles.title: Rays Reveal Starting Pitcher for Game 1 of 2026 World Series vs. Jacob Misiorowski, Brewers
articles.summary: The Tampa Bay Rays have named their starter for Game 1 of the World Series against the Milwaukee Brewers.
articles.body:
The Tampa Bay Rays have named their starter for Game 1 of the World Series against the Milwaukee Brewers.

Nick Martinez, who started once in the divisional series against the New York Yankees and once against the Cleveland Guardians in the ALCS, will be on the bump against Milwaukee and its star ace, Jacob Misiorowski.

Martinez, 36, joined the Rays this offseason and put together one of the best seasons of his career, going 15-6 as he recorded a 3.10 ERA and a 1.09 WHIP with 109 strikeouts.

In a series-clinching Game 3 against the Yankees in the ALDS, Martinez went 3.2 innings, giving up five hits, two runs and a walk while striking out three. In Game 4 against the Guardians in the ALCS, he was credited with the win after pitching 5.1 innings and giving up just two hits and a run with three strikeouts.

Things will only get tougher in the World Series, though, as he faces a Brewers lineup that has recorded the best average (.250) and the most home runs (10) in the postseason so far.

On the hill for the Brewers will be the presumed NL Cy Young Award winner, Misiorowski, who led the majors in ERA (1.80), strikeouts (252) and WHIP (0.80) this year.

He's been a bit dissapointing in the postseason so far, going just 8.1 innings and recording a 3.24 ERA and a 1.56 WHIP through two games. He's had almost two weeks off, though, and should return to the mound ready to shut down the Rays' offense.

Who will come after Martinez in the Rays' rotation remains to be seen, but they'll look for him to put together a solid start to give Tampa Bay an early edge in what should be an exciting series.

articles.title: Hideki Matsui hired as manager of the Yomiuri Giants in Japanese baseball
articles.summary: TOKYO (AP) — Former New York Yankees slugger Hideki Matsui was named Friday as the new manager of the Yomiuri Giants, his club until his departure for the Un...
articles.body:
TOKYO (AP) — Former New York Yankees slugger Hideki Matsui was named Friday as the new manager of the Yomiuri Giants, his club until his departure for the United States.

The 52-year-old Matsui hit a combined 507 home runs in Japan and the United States in a 20-year pro career.

Matsui moved in 2003 to Major League Baseball and spent most of his career with the Yankees.

He batted .282 with 175 home runs and 760 RBIs in MLB . In Japan before that, he hit .304 with 332 home runs and 889 RBSs.

Matsui replaces interim manager Hideki Hashigami, who took over in May after Shinnosuke Abe resigned from the job.
